questions.text:
QUESTION ONE: THE PAN FLUTE

Speed of sound in air = 343 m s⁻¹

The pan flute is a wind instrument that creates sound when air is blown across it. It consists of different length pipes that are bound together. Each pipe is closed at one end and open at the other end.

In the diagram below, draw a diagram of the third harmonic that can be produced in a pan flute. Label nodes (N) and antinodes (A) in the diagram.
questions.expectedAnswer: Diagram showing 3rd harmonic in a closed pipe (3/4 wavelength): node at closed end, antinode at...
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Correct shape with node at closed end and antinode at open end, labelled correctly. Merit: Correct wavelength relationship shown.

questions.text:
Jane has a pan flute. The shortest pipe is 8.50 cm long and the longest pipe is 17.5 cm long.

Calculate the frequency of the third harmonic produced in the shortest pipe.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Correct wavelength OR correct use of v = fλ. Merit: Correct frequency of the third harmonic (3029 Hz) with working shown. For closed pipe, harmonics are odd multiples: L = 3λ/4, so λ = 4L/3 = 4 × 0.085/3 = 0.1133 m. f = v/λ = 343/0.1133 = 3026 Hz (accept 3030 Hz).

questions.text: Explain how standing waves are formed in a pan flute that is open at one end and closed at the other end, and explain why not all harmonics can be formed.
questions.expectedAnswer: Waves reflect off the closed end with 180° phase change, superpose with incident waves to form...
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: ONE of: wave reflects off end; waves in phase produce antinode; quarter wavelengths to have N at closed end. Merit: Identifies odd harmonics and explains quarter wavelength requirement to have N at closed end and A at open end. Excellence: Explains superposition of incident and reflected waves, 180° phase change at closed end, and justifies why only odd multiples of quarter wavelengths (which have nodes at both ends) can form. Accept correct pressure model justification.

questions.text:
Some pan flutes can be tuned by moving a small cork inside the pipe to adjust the length of the pipe. Initially the length of the longest pipe is too long, and the untuned pipe creates a beat of 9.00 Hz with another tuned pipe. The tuned pipe has a length of 0.164 m, which produces a frequency of 523 Hz when playing the first harmonic.

Calculate how much further the cork needs to be pushed into the pipe and explain how it is possible to hear when the cork is in the correct position.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: f₂ = 514 Hz. No beat when in tune. Merit: Correct length of untuned pipe OR explains beat frequency decreases as frequencies get closer (more time between loud regions). Excellence: Correct ΔL calculation AND explains that as f get closer, beat frequency decreases (more time between loud regions) until no beat is heard. Working: f_b = |f₁ − f₂|, 9 = |523 − f₂|, f₂ = 514 Hz (longer pipe = lower frequency). v = fλ, 343 = 514λ, λ = 0.667315 m. L = λ/4 = 0.166829 m. ΔL = 0.166829 − 0.164 = 0.002829 m.

questions.text:
QUESTION TWO: INTERFERENCE

Jane's Physics teacher Mr Smith shines a red laser through a diffraction grating placed at the centre of a semicircular screen. The pattern seen on the screen has a number of narrow, bright fringes.

The formula associated with diffraction gratings is nλ = d sin θ, where n is the order number and λ is the wavelength.

What does the term nλ represent, when n and λ are combined?

The diffraction grating that was used has 200 lines per mm. The red laser used has a wavelength of 638 nm.

Calculate the total number of dots that are seen on the semicircular screen.

Begin your answer by calculating the distance between the slits.
questions.expectedAnswer: 15 dots total (7 on each side plus central maximum).
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Correct value for d = 5 × 10⁻⁶ m. Attempts to use nλ = d sin θ. Merit: One error in calculation OR correct answer of n = 7.83. Excellence: Correct answer of 15 dots in total (must indicate central maxima). NOT 2 × 7.84 = 15.68. Working: d = 1/200000 = 5 × 10⁻⁶ m. nλ = d sin θ, n = d sin θ / λ = 5 × 10⁻⁶ × sin 90° / 638 × 10⁻⁹ = 7.837. Since n is an integer, n_max = 7. Total = 7 + 7 + 1 = 15.

questions.text:
Mr Smith uses the same red laser and shines it through two slits where the slits are of the same width as the diffraction grating, but the slits are further apart. The pattern on the screen is different compared to the pattern obtained in a diffraction grating.

Describe the differences between the patterns formed, and explain the reason for each difference.
questions.expectedAnswer: Two-slit pattern has maxima closer together, less bright, and less well defined than diffraction...
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Identify maxima closer difference OR identify less bright OR identify less well defined. Merit: Justify ONE of: maxima closer together, less bright, less well defined. Excellence: Justify THREE of: maxima closer together (slit separation greater so d sin θ = nλ gives smaller angle), less bright (only two slits so less light passes through), less well defined (only two slits so gradual change from maxima to minima rather than sharp peaks).

questions.text:
Mr Smith then shines white light onto the diffraction grating. The pattern he observes has a central white region, and the other orders form complete spectra on either side of the central white region.

Explain why white light forms a spectra, with violet on the inside and red on the outside, when passed through a diffraction grating.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Identifies blue has shorter wavelength OR red has longer wavelength. Blue has shorter path difference OR red has longer path difference. Merit: Justifies that red is further from central maxima using path difference OR formula. Excellence: Complete answer linking wavelength to path difference to angle for both colours.

questions.text:
QUESTION THREE: DOPPLER EFFECT

Jane and her classmates stand on the platform at a railway station, listening to a train approach them at a constant speed, blowing its whistle. The speed of sound in air is 343 m s⁻¹.

Describe what Jane and her friends would hear, compared to the driver, as the approaching train blows its whistle.
questions.expectedAnswer: Higher frequency / higher pitch than the driver hears.

questions.text: Explain why Jane and her friends would hear a change in frequency as the approaching train blows its whistle.
questions.expectedAnswer: The wave fronts bunch up in front of the approaching train, so apparent wavelength decreases.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: ONE of: wave fronts bunch up so apparent wavelength decreases; speed of sound is constant. Note: NOT waves bunch; NOT speed of train constant. Merit: Wave fronts bunch up, so apparent wavelength decreases AND speed of sound stays the same AND so Jane and her friends will hear a note of higher pitch.

questions.text:
Jane and her friends hear a frequency of 1270 Hz as the train approaches them. After the train has passed them, they hear a frequency of 1190 Hz as the train goes away from them at the same constant speed.

Calculate the speed of the train.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Correct choice of equations for approaching and receding. Note: can cancel f_w together: f(v_w − v_s) = f'(v_w + v_s). Merit: One error in calculation. If incorrectly assumed f = 1230 (midpoint) then v = 10.8 m s⁻¹. Excellence: Correct answer. Working: f_approach = f_w v_w/(v_w − v_s) and f_recede = f_w v_w/(v_w + v_s). So f_approach(v_w − v_s) = f_recede(v_w + v_s). 1270(343 − v_s) = 1190(343 + v_s). 435610 − 1270v_s = 408170 + 1190v_s. 27440 = 2460v_s. v_s = 11.2 m s⁻¹.

questions.text:
Jane and her friends listen to the whistle of another train that approaches them and then goes past them, without stopping at the station. The graph below is a frequency vs position graph for this situation.

Explain what may be happening in this situation by considering the shape of the graph in relation to frequency and position:

(i) as the train approaches (Section A).
questions.expectedAnswer: The graph shows increasing higher pitch
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Identify increasing higher pitch. Merit: Justify increasing higher pitch — the train is accelerating, so the wave fronts bunch up more, decreasing apparent wavelength further and increasing frequency.

questions.text: (ii) as the train is right in front of Jane and her friends (Point B).
questions.expectedAnswer: They hear the actual frequency because there is no component of velocity towards them
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Actual frequency when it is in front of Jane and her friends (the graph line crosses the actual frequency line).

questions.text: (iii) as the train goes away from Jane and her friends (Section C).
questions.expectedAnswer: Decreasing lower pitch as the train recedes,
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Identify decreasing lower pitch. Merit: Justify — the train is accelerating away, so the velocity of the train is increasing relative to Jane, meaning the apparent wavelength increases further and frequency decreases more.
